# Install the CLI

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/install.md

Install `nereus`, the CLI of the platform, on Linux (x86_64 or aarch64); the installer fetches [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) when it is missing.

## Run

Install the latest release:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://getnereus.github.io/install/install.sh | sh
```

Check that it answers:

```bash
nereus --help
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
Usage: nereus [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

  nereus: a composable API platform: reefs add the APIs, Nereids look after
  them, installed at runtime.
```

## What you get

- `nereus`, and `nrs`, the same program under a short name for typing.
- A CLI that upgrades itself in the background; `NEREUS_AUTO_UPGRADE=off` turns that off.
- No cluster yet: the CLI prepares one in the next steps.

## Next

[Write the settings](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/settings/) of your first installation.

# Write the settings

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/settings.md

Choose the settings of your first installation and keep them in a file, before any cluster exists.

## Run

See what [`nereus init`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#init-dry-run) would use, and where each value comes from; `--dry-run` creates nothing:

```bash
nereus init --dry-run --create-cluster
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
SETTING            VALUE   SOURCE
target             k3d     default
create_cluster     true    flag
name               nereus  default
ingress_port       8080    default
installation_name  nereus  cluster name
profile            core    default
```

The table comes first; the two `helm upgrade --install` lines after it make the same install by hand.

Write the same settings to a file with [`nereus init --generate-file`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#init-generate-file); it prints the table again and the path it wrote:

```bash
nereus init --generate-file --create-cluster
```

Read the file:

```bash
cat ~/.config/nereus/init.yaml
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: InitConfig
spec:
  profile: core
  ingressPort: 8080
  undercloud:
    create: true
    name: nereus
---
apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Installation
metadata:
  name: nereus
spec:
  alias: nereus
```

## What you get

- Two documents: the `InitConfig`, how this machine builds the platform, and the `Installation`, whose name never changes ([spec 0006](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/0006-installation-identity/)).
- The profile `core`: core and the tenancy Reef, nothing more until you add it ([Runtime and profiles](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/runtime-and-profiles/)).
- A plain `nereus init` reads this file; a flag wins over it, and an unknown key is an error.
- Nothing created yet: no cluster, no registry.

## Next

[Prepare the cluster](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init/) from these settings.

# Prepare the cluster

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init.md

Create a local k3d cluster and install core on it, from the settings you wrote.

## Run

`init` needs Docker 20.10.5 or newer with its daemon running, k3d 5.0.0 or newer and Helm 4.0.0 or newer; it checks them first and stops before changing anything when one is missing, naming the version it needs.

Prepare the cluster without being asked to confirm: [`nereus init`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#init)

```bash
nereus init --yes
```

It prints the settings table, then one line per step with its time: the prerequisites, the local registry, the cluster, the kinds, the Nereus API and the installation. It ends with `cluster ready in context k3d-nereus` and names `nereus status` as the next step.

## What you get

- A k3d cluster `nereus`, its local registry on `localhost:5111`, and your kube context pointing at it.
- Core: the kinds of the [model](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/), the [Nereus API](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/nereus-api/) and the tenancy Reef; no Nereid yet.
- The installation's identity: its name and a random id, which the first `init` also writes into the settings file, so a cluster recreated from it is the same installation.
- `~/.config/nereus/values.yaml`: the values `init` passed to Helm, to run the same install by hand.
- The total time, measured against the SLO: 8 minutes on k3d.

## Next

[Look around](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/look-around/) the new installation.

# Look around

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/look-around.md

See what the new installation holds before you add anything: its Reefs and the Nereids that look after them.

## Run

See how each Reef is doing, one row per Reef and Nereid: [`nereus status`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#status)

```bash
nereus status
```

On core alone there are two rows, `core` and `tenancy`, both `Ready`.

List the Reefs: [`nereus reef list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#reef-list)

```bash
nereus reef list
```

`tenancy` is the only one, with `-` under `NEREIDS`: the Nereus API keeps its objects itself, so no Nereid serves it.

List the Nereids: [`nereus nereid list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#nereid-list)

```bash
nereus nereid list
```

There are none yet; the line it prints points to `nereus nereid apply --help`.

## What you get

- A map of the installation: a Reef is a capability with its own API group, a Nereid is the controller that looks after it ([Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/)).
- These commands read the cluster with your kubeconfig, since core alone offers no sign-in; once an installation has the authentication Reef, they read through the Nereus API and ask for `nereus login` first.

## Next

[Apply a Reef and its Nereid](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/first-reef/).

# Apply a reef and its Nereid

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/first-reef.md

Add the release Reef, the reference Nereid that serves it, and the Mandate that makes that Nereid the Reef's answer.

## Run

Apply the Reef, from the version this CLI pins: [`nereus reef apply release`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#reef-apply)

```bash
nereus reef apply release
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/reefs/release 0.1.0 created (release.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1: releases, repositories, sources, targets)

Next steps:

  nereus release --help
  nereus nereid apply <nereid> --reef release
```

Apply the reference Nereid, which answers every command of the Reef with no tool behind it: [`nereus nereid apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#nereid-apply)

```bash
nereus nereid apply reference-release
```

The CLI reads the Reef from the image's label, pins the image to its digest and waits until the Nereid reports `Ready`; its next step names the Mandate below.

Bind the Reef to it, as the Reef's default: [`nereus mandate create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#mandate-create)

```bash
nereus mandate create reference --reef release --nereid reference-release --default
```

It prints `core/mandates/reference created (reef: release, nereid: reference-release, default)`.

## What you get

- The Reef `release`, with its four kinds, and a `release` command group in the CLI: `nereus release --help` lists the commands its Nereid published.
- The Nereid `reference-release`, running in the cluster as the Reef's controller.
- The Mandate `reference`, which sends every request of the Reef to that Nereid ([Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/)).

## Next

[Run its commands](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/run/).

# Run its commands

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/run.md

Use the `release` group the reference Nereid published: add a Helm repository and list it.

## Run

See the group's commands; the CLI built them from what the Nereid published, with no code downloaded:

```bash
nereus release --help
```

It lists one group per kind of the Reef: `repository`, `source` and `target`, next to the releases themselves.

Add a Helm repository: [`nereus release repository create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/release.html#repository-create)

```bash
nereus release repository create codecentric \
  --url https://codecentric.github.io/helm-charts \
  --type http
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ release/repositories/codecentric created
NAME         TYPE  URL                                        READY
codecentric  http  https://codecentric.github.io/helm-charts  True

Next steps:

  nereus release source create <name> --repository codecentric --chart <chart> --version <version>
```

List the repositories: [`nereus release repository list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/release.html#repository-list)

```bash
nereus release repository list
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
NAME         TYPE  URL                                        READY
codecentric  http  https://codecentric.github.io/helm-charts  True
```

## What you get

- A `Repository` object in the cluster, `Ready`: the reference Nereid answered it with no tool behind it.
- The group is named after the Reef, not the Nereid: another Nereid of `release` would serve the same commands ([Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/)).

## Next

[Clean up](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/clean-up/) when you are done.

# Clean up

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/clean-up.md

Delete the Nereid, then the cluster and its local registry, so the machine is as it was before `init`.

## Run

Delete the Nereid: [`nereus nereid delete`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#nereid-delete)

```bash
nereus nereid delete reference-release
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/nereids/reference-release deleted
```

Delete the cluster, with everything `init` installed in it:

```bash
k3d cluster delete nereus
```

Delete the local registry `init` created next to it:

```bash
k3d registry delete k3d-nereus-registry.localhost
```

## What you get

- The `release` command group goes with the Nereid, and its Deployment, Service and identity with it; the Reef stays until the cluster goes.
- No cluster and no registry left.
- The settings stay in `~/.config/nereus/`: a next `nereus init --yes` creates a cluster that is the same installation, with the same id. Delete that folder to start from nothing.

## Next

Learn the words behind what you ran: [Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/).

# What Nereus is

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/what-is-nereus.md

Nereus is a composable API platform: Reefs add the APIs, Nereids look after them, both installed at runtime, and one API and one CLI serve them all.

## Example

`nereus --help` groups the commands: the platform's own, the model's, and one group per Reef the installation knows:

```bash
nereus --help
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
Usage: nereus [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

  nereus: a composable API platform: reefs add the APIs, Nereids look after
  them, installed at runtime.

Model:
  mandate         Mandates: each binds one reef to one Nereid.
  nereid          Nereids: the controllers that look after reefs.
  reef            Reefs: the capabilities of the platform, each an API group.
  user            Users: one per person, whatever the login.

Reefs:
  authentication  Reef authentication, looked after by nereid keycloak.
  release         Reef release, looked after by nereid flux.
  secrets         Reef secrets, looked after by nereid openbao.
```

## Overview

<!-- diagram:architecture:end -->

*One installation: the control plane reconciles the environments, beside the services it uses, on any infrastructure.*

## How it works

- The engine is `core`, the kinds `Reef`, `Nereid`, `Mandate` and `Profile`, and nothing else; the words are in [Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/).
- Every capability arrives at runtime as a Reef, and a Nereid fills it with the tool you pick ([Runtime install and profiles](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/runtime-and-profiles/)).
- The CLI, the portal and agents go through one door, [the Nereus API](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/nereus-api/), and never name a tool.
- Swapping a tool means adding another Nereid to the Reef and moving its default Mandate: no command, client or app declaration changes.
- Whose each thing is, and who may act on it, belongs to the platform itself ([Tenancy and access](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/tenancy-and-access/)).

## Not this

- Not only an Internal Developer Platform: that is one profile, `internal-developer-platform`; a Reef can serve any recurring knowledge work.
- Not a portal: the portal is one Reef, `portal`, and one client of the API.
- Not a wrapper around one tool: Flux, Keycloak or OpenBao stay behind a Nereid, and a Reef outlives the tool.
- Not a replacement for Kubernetes: it runs on a cluster, and each Reef is an API group there.

## Next

[Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/): the three words the rest of the docs use.

# Reef, Nereid and Mandate

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model.md

A Reef is a capability of the platform, a Nereid is the controller that looks after it, and a Mandate binds one Reef to one Nereid.

## Example

`nereus --help` lists each Reef installed with the Nereid that looks after it:

``` { .text .output title="output" }
Reefs:
  release         Reef release, looked after by nereid flux.
  secrets         Reef secrets, looked after by nereid openbao.
```

The secrets Reef adds the kinds `Vault` and `Secret` and the commands `nereus secrets ...`; the Mandate `default` says that `openbao` keeps them.

## Overview

<!-- diagram:model:start (scripts/docs/diagrams) -->
<figure class="diagram model" markdown="0">

</figure>
<!-- diagram:model:end -->

*The CLI speaks to the Reef; the Mandate names the Nereid that does the work with its tool.*

## How it works

- A Reef is an API group, `<reef>.getnereus.dev`, with its own kinds; [`nereus reef apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#reef-apply) adds one at runtime.
- A Nereid is a Kubernetes controller that reconciles the Reef's objects and writes their `status`.
- A Mandate binds one Reef to one Nereid; one Mandate per Reef is the default, and its commands go there.
- Several Nereids can look after one Reef (`keycloak` or `auth0` for authentication): you pick one per Mandate.
- Each Reef adds its own commands to the CLI, so `nereus --help` grows with the installation.

## Not this

- A Reef is not a Helm chart: it is the API; the Nereid brings the software behind it.
- A Nereid is not the tool itself: `openbao` is the controller, OpenBao is what it drives.

## Next

[Runtime install and profiles](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/runtime-and-profiles/): how Reefs and Nereids arrive in a running installation.

# Runtime install and profiles

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/runtime-and-profiles.md

Nereus installs its capabilities at runtime: `nereus init` lays down the engine, `core`, and a profile is a named list of Reefs, Nereids and Mandates applied on top of it.

## Example

[`nereus profile describe`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#profile-describe) shows what a profile installs, in order, each Nereid with its Reef and its Mandate:

```bash
nereus profile describe secrets
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
NEREID   REEF     MANDATE            REQUIRED BY
openbao  secrets  default (default)  -
```

## Overview

<!-- diagram:runtime:end -->

*Init lays down core; a profile, or a person one command at a time, adds the rest.*

## How it works

- [`nereus init`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#init) installs the kinds, the namespace, the Nereus API, core and the tenancy Reef with Helm; the profile `core`, the default, installs nothing more.
- [`nereus init --profile internal-developer-platform`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#init-profile) adds a profile: the Nereid `thetis` installs its Reefs, Nereids and Mandates, and `init` waits until they are Ready.
- A profile never writes the order: each Nereid comes after the Nereids of the Reefs it requires, read from its image's label `core.getnereus.dev/requires`.
- A profile adds nothing the commands cannot do: `nereus reef apply`, `nereus nereid apply` and `nereus mandate create` do the same by hand, on a running installation.
- A profile never carries a secret: credentials reach a Nereid through the secrets Reef, encrypted on the client, once the profile is installed.

## Not this

- Not a fixed install: Reefs and Nereids come and go on a running installation, and init never has to run again for them.
- Not a size: profiles are named by purpose, never `minimal` or `full`; `core` alone is the default, so a plain init stays fast.
- Not access: who may do what is a role, in [Tenancy and access](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/tenancy-and-access/).

## Next

[Undercloud and overcloud](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/undercloud-overcloud/): where an installation starts when its home is a cloud.

# Undercloud and overcloud

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/undercloud-overcloud.md

The undercloud is the local k3d cluster that seeds an installation and bootstraps its cloud; the overcloud is the cloud cluster, AKS first, the platform then moves into, still as one installation.

[planned #61]

## Example

A cloud in the settings file makes `nereus init` create the undercloud, `tailwind-undercloud`, instead of a plain local cluster:

```yaml
apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: InitConfig
spec:
  cloud: azure
---
apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Installation
metadata:
  name: tailwind
spec:
  alias: tailwind
```

## Overview

</figure>
<!-- diagram:undercloud:end -->

*The undercloud gets the cloud to trust it, then hands the platform to the overcloud.*

## How it works

- [`nereus init --target azure`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#init-target) computes the cluster's OIDC issuer from the installation's id before the cluster exists, then installs the `cloud` Reef and its `azure` Nereid.
- The Nereid plans the bootstrap (the names, the issuer storage, the issuer documents, the first identity); the CLI shows the plan and runs it with your own login once you approve.
- From then on the cloud trusts the cluster's tokens through workload identity federation, so the platform keeps no secret.
- The pivot moves the platform to the overcloud, as Cluster API's `clusterctl move` does, moves the federated credential to the overcloud's issuer, then deletes the undercloud [planned #61].
- Both are one installation: the same name, id and identities; only the cluster role label, `core.getnereus.dev/cluster-role`, stays with each cluster.

## Not this

- Not two installations, nor staging and production: one platform on two clusters, one after the other.
- Not a management cluster kept forever: the undercloud is deleted after the pivot.
- Not needed on a laptop: a plain `nereus init` with no cloud makes a cluster named `nereus`, with no undercloud role.

## Next

[Tenancy and access](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/tenancy-and-access/): whose each thing is, and who may do what.

# Tenancy and access

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/tenancy-and-access.md

Tenancy says whose each thing is, a tree of Organizations and nested Projects; access says who may do what on a node of that tree, through roles bound to teams.

## Example

The tree is two kinds of the tenancy Reef, applied with [`nereus tenancy apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/tenancy.html#apply):

```yaml
apiVersion: tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Organization
metadata:
  name: example
---
apiVersion: tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Project
metadata:
  name: payments
spec:
  parent: {kind: Organization, name: example}
```

## Overview

<svg class="rh narrow" viewBox="0 0 360 392" role="img" aria-label="In the Organization example, a Binding gives the Role developer to the Team payments on the Project payments; the Nereus API asks the Binding whether a User may act."><rect class="zone" x="0" y="0" width="360" height="296"/><text class="h" x="12" y="30" text-anchor="start">Organization</text><text class="m" x="348" y="30" text-anchor="end">(example)</text><rect class="card" x="12" y="48" width="336" height="56"/><text class="b" x="180" y="72" text-anchor="middle">Project payments</text><text class="s" x="180" y="92" text-anchor="middle">(a node of the tree)</text><rect class="card" x="12" y="136" width="336" height="56"/><text class="b" x="180" y="160" text-anchor="middle">Team payments</text><text class="s" x="180" y="180" text-anchor="middle">(its members)</text><line class="ln" x1="180" y1="136" x2="180" y2="104"/><polygon class="ah" points="175.1,112.4 184.9,112.4 180,104"/><rect class="card" x="12" y="224" width="336" height="56"/><text class="b" x="180" y="248" text-anchor="middle">Binding</text><text class="s" x="180" y="268" text-anchor="middle">(gives a Role on the Project)</text><line class="ln" x1="180" y1="224" x2="180" y2="192"/><polygon class="ah" points="175.1,200.4 184.9,200.4 180,192"/><rect class="actor" x="0" y="336" width="174" height="56"/><text class="b" x="87" y="369" text-anchor="middle">Role developer</text><line class="ln" x1="87" y1="280" x2="87" y2="336"/><polygon class="ah" points="82.1,327.6 91.9,327.6 87,336"/><rect class="actor" x="186" y="336" width="174" height="56"/><text class="b" x="273" y="369" text-anchor="middle">Nereus API</text><line class="ln dashed" x1="273" y1="336" x2="273" y2="280"/><polygon class="ah" points="268.1,288.4 277.9,288.4 273,280"/><text class="lbl" x="265" y="316" text-anchor="end">may this User?</text></svg>
</figure>
<!-- diagram:tenancy:end -->

*A binding gives a role to a team on one node; the API asks before it acts.*

## How it works

- Tenancy is a Reef, `tenancy.getnereus.dev`, whose kinds come from each instance: every kind is a node with an optional `spec.parent`, and one kind, the boundary, isolates people and billing (here `Organization`).
- Whatever belongs somewhere names `owner: {kind, name}` in the tree: a Workload, an Environment, a team.
- The `authorization` Reef holds access: a `Role` is a list of rules, `<reef>:<kinds>:<verbs>`, and a `Binding` gives it to a team, a position in a team or, as the exception, one User, on one node; access flows down the tree.
- The `teams` Reef keeps one list of members: joining a team grants its access, leaving removes it. A person is one core `User` whatever the login, and a login with no User has no permission.
- The Nereus API asks before it acts; [`nereus can-i`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/authorization.html#can-i-yes) asks the same question and names the binding that grants it.

## Not this

- A Project is not a Kubernetes namespace: it nests, and one Project runs in several environments, on several clusters.
- A team is not an identity provider's group: groups are an output a Nereid may write, never the source.
- A role is not a profile: a [profile](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/runtime-and-profiles/) is what an installation installs.

## Next

[The Nereus API](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/nereus-api/): the door every client goes through.

# The Nereus API

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/nereus-api.md

The Nereus API is the platform's one door: the CLI, the portal, an IDE and agents talk to it with the person's token, and the Kubernetes API, the Nereids and their tools stay behind it.

## Example

[`nereus whoami`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/authentication.html#whoami) asks the API's first route, `GET /v1/me`, instead of reading the local token:

```bash
nereus whoami --help
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
Usage: nereus whoami [OPTIONS]

  Who you are, as the Nereus API answers (GET /v1/me) for the token of nereus
  login, never what the local token says: the login, and the User of Nereus
  behind it (#1645), or that there is none yet.
```

## Overview

<!-- diagram:nereus-api:start (scripts/docs/diagrams) -->

y="432" text-anchor="middle">(OpenBao, GitHub, a cloud)</text><line class="ln" x1="180" y1="344" x2="180" y2="392"/><polygon class="ah" points="175.1,383.6 184.9,383.6 180,392"/></svg>
