[`nereus secrets binding create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/secrets.html#binding-create) makes the Kubernetes Secret in the namespace from the secret's current version; each `--key NAME=KEY` renames a key, and without any, every key keeps its own name. A namespace the vault does not allow, or a key the secret lacks, is refused before anything is written.

```bash
nereus secrets binding create keycloak-google \
  --secret default/google-oauth \
  --namespace identity \
  --key client-id=GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID \
  --key client-secret=GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ secrets/vaults/default/secrets/google-oauth/secretbindings/identity/keycloak-google created
Secret keycloak-google ready in namespace identity.

Next steps:

  nereus secrets binding get keycloak-google --namespace identity
```

A chart asks the same way, with a SecretBinding among its templates, as `test/charts/binding-demo` does; `helm uninstall` removes it and its Kubernetes Secret. A [release](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/release/) asks with `--secret`.

## Check it worked

[`nereus secrets binding list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/secrets.html#binding-list) shows each binding with `FOR`, who asked: a release, a chart from its Helm labels, or the CLI user.

```bash
nereus secrets binding list
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
NAME             SECRET                NAMESPACE  FOR                 STATUS  AGE
keycloak-google  default/google-oauth  identity   system:admin        Ready   12s
binding-demo     default/google-oauth  tools      chart binding-demo  Ready   4s
```

A secret is not deleted while bindings use it: [`nereus secrets get`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/secrets.html#binding-used) lists them.

## Clean up

[`nereus secrets binding delete`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/secrets.html#binding-delete) deletes the Kubernetes Secret first, then the binding.

```bash
nereus secrets binding delete keycloak-google \
  --namespace identity
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ secrets/vaults/default/secrets/google-oauth/secretbindings/identity/keycloak-google deleted

Next steps:

  nereus secrets binding list --namespace identity
```

## Next

- [Release a chart](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/release/) that reads the secret through a binding.
- Give a team a vault of its own with [`nereus secrets vault create --allow-namespace`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/secrets.html#vault-create).

## Learn more

- [The secrets Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/secrets/): vaults, secrets and bindings, every command.

# Release a chart

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/release.md

Release a Helm chart into a namespace, with its values and its secrets, through the Nereid that its [Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/) picks: Flux here, swappable for another tool.

## Before you start

- A cluster from [Prepare the cluster](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init/) with `--profile internal-developer-platform`: it brings the release Reef with the Nereid `flux` as its default, and the secrets Reef.
- A secret `google-oauth` from [Keep a secret](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/secrets/), in a vault that allows the target's namespace.
- A file `keycloak-values.yaml` with the chart's values.

## Steps

### 1. Point at the chart repository

A [`Repository`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/release.html#repository-create) says where charts come from: `http` for a Helm repository, `oci` for a registry.

```bash
nereus release repository create codecentric \
  --url https://codecentric.github.io/helm-charts \
  --type http
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ release/repositories/codecentric created
NAME         TYPE  URL                                        READY
codecentric  http  https://codecentric.github.io/helm-charts  True

Next steps:

  nereus release source create <name> --repository codecentric --chart <chart> --version <version>
```

### 2. Pick the chart and its version

A [`Source`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/release.html#source-create) is one chart at one version.

```bash
nereus release source create keycloak \
  --repository codecentric \
  --chart keycloakx \
  --version 7.0.1
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ release/sources/keycloak created
NAME      REPOSITORY   CHART      VERSION  DIGEST  READY
keycloak  codecentric  keycloakx  7.0.1    -       True

Next steps:

  nereus release target create <name> --namespace <namespace>
```

### 3. Say where it goes

A [`Target`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/release.html#target-create) is a namespace, made when missing. `--environment` picks an environment of the environment Reef; without it, the target is in the cluster Nereus runs in.

```bash
nereus release target create dev-identity \
  --environment dev \
  --namespace identity
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ release/targets/dev-identity created
NAME          ENVIRONMENT  NAMESPACE  READY
dev-identity  dev          identity   True

Next steps:

  nereus release create <name> --source <source> --target dev-identity
```

### 4. Release it with its values and secrets

[`nereus release create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/release.html#release-create-secrets) puts the source in the target. `--secret` makes a Kubernetes Secret with every key of a secret in the target's namespace; `--secret-value <path>=<secret>/<key>` puts one key into one values field. The CLI refuses a vault that does not allow the namespace before writing anything.

```bash
nereus release create keycloak \
  --source keycloak \
  --target dev-identity \
  --values-file keycloak-values.yaml \
  --mandate flux \
  --secret google-oauth \
  --secret-value nereus.googleClientId=google-oauth/GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ release/releases/keycloak created (nereid: flux)
  binding secrets/vaults/default/secrets/google-oauth/secretbindings/identity/keycloak
  binding secrets/vaults/default/secrets/google-oauth/secretbindings/nereus-system/keycloak-values-google-oauth

Next steps:

  nereus release get keycloak --watch
```

## Check it worked

[`nereus release get --watch`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/release.html#release-create-secrets) follows the release: the secret bindings first, then the chart, until it is `Ready`.

```bash
nereus release get keycloak \
  --watch
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
NAME      SOURCE    TARGET        VERSION  NEREID             STATUS
keycloak  keycloak  dev-identity  7.0.1    flux    Pending
2026-10-30T07:53:21Z  ✓ binding      2 Secrets ready: identity/keycloak, nereus-system/keycloak-values-google-oauth.
2026-10-30T07:53:21Z  ✓ helmrelease  Wrote the Flux HelmRelease keycloak.
keycloak  keycloak  dev-identity  7.0.1    flux    Progressing
keycloak  keycloak  dev-identity  7.0.1    flux    Ready
```

A release that fails shows `Failed` once Flux stops retrying; a refused namespace or a failed binding shows `BindingFailed`.

## Next

- [Run a registry](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/registry/) to publish your own chart with [`nereus release source publish`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/release.html#source-publish).
- [Follow the golden path](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/golden-path/): your own image, deployed through a ready-made chart into an Environment of its own.

## Learn more

- [The release Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/release/): repositories, sources, targets and releases, every command.
- [Runtime and profiles](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/runtime-and-profiles/): why the Mandate, not the Reef, picks Flux.

# Run a registry

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/registry.md

Run a [zot](https://zotregistry.dev) registry of your own in the cluster, publish an image to it and run that image: TLS only, nothing anonymous, images kept on its own volume.

## Before you start

- A cluster from [Prepare the cluster](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init/) with `--profile internal-developer-platform`: it brings the registry Reef with the Nereid `zot`, the release Reef that installs zot, and the secrets Reef that keeps each registry's read credential.
- `nereus login` done: publishing pushes through the Nereus API, for a person in `nereus-admins`.
- The namespace `builds`, which `nereus nereid apply buildkit --reef build` makes: each repository's push identity lives there.
- An image built locally with a tag, such as `docker build --tag hello:v1 .`.
- A k3d cluster: on AKS the registry Reef is [planned], since the nodes pull only from registries whose certificate they trust, and they do not trust the CA of a registry in the cluster ([Prepare a cluster for Nereus](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/operate/cluster/)).

## Steps

### 1. Create a registry

[`nereus registry create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/registry.html#registry-create) makes a namespace `registry-<name>` with zot and a 10 GiB volume. The first registry also makes the vault `registries`. `--purge-unused` is optional: it deletes each image no Delivery runs once older than the duration, keeping the newest of each repository.

```bash
nereus registry create main \
  --purge-unused 168h
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
secrets/vaults/registries created
registry/registries/main created (mandate: zot, nereid: zot; purge: images no Delivery runs, after 168h)
```

### 2. Publish an image

[`nereus registry repository publish`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/registry.html#repository-publish) creates the repository with a push identity of its own and pushes the local image through the Nereus API with your login; your docker configuration stays untouched. A tag is published once: the same tag again is refused.

```bash
nereus registry repository publish hello \
  --registry main \
  --image hello:v1
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
registry/registries/main/repositories/hello created
registry/registries/main/repositories/hello/tags/v1 published (sha256:97683bd68ee3e86c6560172b9f6e0b371a6bbcebf06041dbe7284355a7703797)

Next steps:

  nereus workload deploy hello@<environment> --image localhost:30763/hello:v1
```

### 3. Run it

[`nereus workload deploy`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/delivery.html#workload-deploy) runs the image in an Environment, here `dev` from [Follow the golden path](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/golden-path/). Name the address the publish printed; the Pod runs the digest found behind the tag. A registry with an owner serves only a Workload and an Environment of that owner or under it in the [tenancy tree](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/tenancy-and-access/).

```bash
nereus workload deploy hello@dev \
  --image localhost:30763/hello:v1 \
  --wait
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ delivery/deliveries/hello-dev configured
✓ delivery/deliveries/hello-dev ready (sha256:de1338)

Next steps:

  nereus workload logs hello-dev
```

## Check it worked

[`nereus registry get`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/registry.html#registry-get) shows the registry ready, its pull address for the nodes and the credential that reads it.

```bash
nereus registry get main
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
NAME  NEREID  PURGE  PULL-ADDRESS     READY
main  zot     168h   localhost:30763  True

credential: secret registries/main-pull (vault registries)

localhost:30763 is a NodePort, for an image reference on this cluster's nodes. Reading it takes the credential above.
```

## Clean up

!!! warning "Deleted for good"
    The registry's namespace and volume go with it, and every image on the volume.

A repository that a Delivery runs is refused, and so is a registry that still has repositories: delete the Deliveries first.

```bash
nereus registry repository delete hello
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✗ registry/repositories/hello is still in use by delivery/deliveries/hello-dev. To delete it, run:
  # first, the Deliveries that run its images
  nereus delivery delete hello-dev
  nereus registry repository delete hello
```

```bash
nereus registry delete main
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
registry/registries/main deleted

Next steps:

  nereus registry list
```

## Next

- [Follow the golden path](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/golden-path/): an Environment of your own, and a Workload deployed into it.
- Run what a Build pushed: [`nereus workload deploy --build`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/delivery.html#deploy-build) takes the Build's digest instead of a tag.

## Learn more

- [The registry Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/registry/): registries, repositories, purge and every command.
- [Tenancy and access](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/tenancy-and-access/): who may read a registry with an owner.

# Say what Nereus has

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/catalog.md

Register what a repository says it runs and publishes, Workloads and Packages, from its files in `catalog/`, and check that it holds together: the files are the truth, the catalog Reef holds a copy.

## Before you start

- A cluster from [Prepare the cluster](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init/) with `--profile internal-developer-platform`: it brings the catalog Reef with its Nereid `catalog`, which writes each entry's status and changes nothing an entry names.
- The [tenancy tree](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/access/tenancy/) the entries name as owners.
- A checkout with a `catalog/` folder, such as Nereus's own.

## Steps

### 1. Register the repository's catalog

[`nereus catalog apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/catalog.html#workload-apply) takes the folder, types first, then the entries. An owner that does not exist, or a registry a type does not take, refuses the whole folder; a second run prints `unchanged`.

```bash
nereus catalog apply \
  --from-file catalog/
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ catalog/workloadtypes/controller created
✓ catalog/workloadtypes/service created
✓ catalog/packagetypes/cli created
✓ catalog/packagetypes/image created
✓ catalog/workloads/flux created (owner: Project/nereids, type: controller)
✓ catalog/workloads/keycloak created (owner: Project/nereids, type: controller)
✓ catalog/workloads/openbao created (owner: Project/nereids, type: controller)
✓ catalog/workloads/triton created (owner: Project/triton, type: service)
✓ catalog/packages/nereus created (owner: Project/core, type: cli, registry: pypi)
✓ catalog/packages/openbao-image created (owner: Project/nereids, type: image, registry: oci)

Next steps:

  nereus catalog check
```

### 2. Write a new entry as a file

[`nereus catalog workload create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/catalog.html#workload-create) with `--dry-run --output yaml` prints the file to commit in `catalog/`, then apply. `--audience` is required: `none` says nobody talks to it. Without `--owner`, the owner set by [`nereus config set owner`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/tenancy.html#config-owner) is used.

```bash
nereus catalog workload create edge-cloudflare \
  --type controller \
  --audience none \
  --ref branch=main \
  --dry-run \
  --output yaml
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
apiVersion: catalog.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Workload
metadata:
  name: edge-cloudflare
spec:
  owner:
    kind: Project
    name: nereids
  type: controller
  source:
    ref:
      branch: main
```

### 3. Check that it holds together

[`nereus catalog check`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/catalog.html#check) fails with `✗` on a contradiction, such as an owner whose Project was deleted; a gap prints `!` with its issue and passes. A lookup that did not run is a gap, never a pass.

```bash
nereus catalog check
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ tenancy: 1 organization, 5 projects, every owner resolves
✓ types: every workload type and package type resolves, every registry allowed
! catalog/workloads/triton: audience people, agents, no edge reef (#470)
! catalog/workloads/triton: uses nats, no messaging reef (#576)
! catalog/packages/nereus: not found on pypi
0 contradictions, 3 gaps
```

`make catalog-check` runs it on the repository's files before a pull request, with a cluster that has the tenancy Reef.

## Check it worked

[`nereus catalog list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/catalog.html#workload-list) shows each Workload with what the catalog Nereid found, `-` until its first pass.

```bash
nereus catalog list
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
WORKLOAD  OWNER            TYPE        AUDIENCE        STATUS
catalog   Project/nereids  controller  -               Ready
flux      Project/nereids  controller  -               NereidNotInstalled
keycloak  Project/nereids  controller  -               NereidNotInstalled
openbao   Project/nereids  controller  -               NereidNotInstalled
triton    Project/triton   service     agents, people  DeploymentNotFound
```

## Next

- [Follow the golden path](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/golden-path/): a Workload deployed into an Environment of its own.

## Learn more

- [The catalog Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/catalog/): Workloads, Packages, their types, every status and command.
- [ADR 0016](https://docs.getnereus.dev/adr/0016-catalog-reef/): the files in the repository are the truth, the cluster holds a copy.

# Follow the golden path

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/golden-path.md

Run your own image in an Environment of its own, a vcluster, from `docker build` to a Pod that answers, through a ready-made chart and with no product code.

## Before you start

- A cluster from [Prepare the cluster](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init/) with `--profile internal-developer-platform`, and `nereus login` done: it brings the environment Reef with the Nereid `vcluster`, the catalog, the delivery Reef with the Nereid `kubernetes`, and the release Reef with `flux`.
- The workload type `service` from the repository's catalog, as in [Say what Nereus has](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/catalog/).
- Your image pushed to the registry that `nereus status` names, such as `docker build --tag localhost:5111/hello:0.1.0 test/golden-path`, then `docker push localhost:5111/hello:0.1.0`. The same reference pushes and pulls, from your machine and from the nodes.

## Steps

### 1. Get an Environment

[`nereus environment create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/environment.html#create) makes a vcluster for an owner, deleted when it expires. It is `small` unless its Mandate says otherwise: 20 Pods, 512Mi per container. Its Pods reach one another and the Internet, never the platform's own Services.

```bash
nereus environment create dev \
  --owner project/nereus \
  --expires 2h
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ environment/environments/dev created (mandate: vcluster, nereid: vcluster)

Next steps:

  nereus environment get dev --watch
  nereus environment kubeconfig dev
```

### 2. Say what runs

A Workload is the catalog's entry: who owns it, its type and who talks to it. [`nereus workload create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/catalog.html#workload-create) is short for `nereus catalog workload create`.

```bash
nereus workload create hello \
  --owner project/nereids \
  --type service \
  --audience programs
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ catalog/workloads/hello created (owner: Project/nereids, type: service)

Next steps:

  nereus catalog workload list
```

### 3. Deploy it

[`nereus workload deploy`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/delivery.html#workload-deploy) takes `hello@dev`, the Workload and the Environment: a bare `hello` is refused, since a deploy always says where it goes. The Nereid `kubernetes` resolves the tag to a digest, reads the port the image exposes, and releases a ready-made chart in the vcluster.

```bash
nereus workload deploy hello@dev \
  --image localhost:5111/hello:0.1.0
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ delivery/deliveries/hello-dev created

Next steps:

  nereus delivery get hello-dev
```

A tag moves only with a deploy: push the same tag with other content and deploy again for a new digest, the previous one kept. `--wait` waits on the deploy and prints the Nereid's reason when it cannot deliver.

## Check it worked

[`nereus delivery get --watch`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/delivery.html#delivery-get) follows the Delivery until its Pod is ready.

```bash
nereus delivery get hello-dev \
  --watch
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
NAME       WORKLOAD  ENVIRONMENT  DIGEST  NAMESPACE  READY
hello-dev  hello     dev          -       -          Unknown
hello-dev  hello     dev          sha256:fdeec3  hello-dev  False
hello-dev  hello     dev          sha256:fdeec3  hello-dev  True

Next steps:

  nereus workload logs hello-dev
```

[`nereus workload logs`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/delivery.html#workload-logs) reads the Pods' output through the Nereus API, with no kubeconfig and no port-forward of yours; `--follow` stays until Ctrl+C.

```bash
nereus workload logs hello-dev
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:53792: response:200
```

## Clean up

!!! warning "Deleted for good"
    Deleting the Environment deletes its vcluster and everything inside it.

Delete the Delivery first: an Environment that a Delivery still targets is refused. [`nereus delivery delete`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/delivery.html#delivery-delete) removes its Release, so Flux uninstalls the chart.

```bash
nereus delivery delete hello-dev \
  --timeout 300
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
2026-11-04T17:26:05Z  … release  Deleting release/releases/hello-dev: Flux uninstalls the chart.
2026-11-04T17:26:06Z  · target   Deleting release/targets/hello-dev.
2026-11-04T17:26:38Z  ✓ release  release/releases/hello-dev deleted.
2026-11-04T17:26:37Z  … target   Deleting release/targets/hello-dev.
✓ delivery/deliveries/hello-dev deleted

Next steps:

  nereus workload list
```

```bash
nereus environment delete dev \
  --timeout 600
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
2026-11-04T17:26:47Z  … release    Deleting release/releases/env-dev: Flux uninstalls the vcluster chart.
2026-11-04T17:26:47Z  · namespace  Deleting the namespace env-vcluster-dev.
2026-11-04T17:27:15Z  ✓ release    release/releases/env-dev deleted.
2026-11-04T17:27:14Z  … namespace  Deleting the namespace env-vcluster-dev.
✓ environment/environments/dev deleted

Next steps:

  nereus environment list
```

## Next

- [Run a registry](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/registry/) of your own, and deploy from it.
- [Collect metrics](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/metrics/): see how each Nereid is doing.

## Learn more

- [The environment Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/environment/): sizes, expiry, kubeconfig and every command.
- [The delivery Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/delivery/): Deliveries, the chart they release and why one fails.

# Collect metrics

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/metrics.md

See how each Nereid is doing, its passes, failures and how long a pass takes, in the metrics the platform keeps with [VictoriaMetrics](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/).

## Before you start

- A cluster from [Prepare the cluster](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init/) with `--profile internal-developer-platform`: it brings the metrics Reef with the Nereid `victoriametrics`, which scrapes every Nereid in `nereus-system` and each node's CPU and memory per container.
- `kubectl` reaching that cluster. The query API has no credentials yet, so only the scraper, the Nereus API and a port-forward reach it.

## Steps

### 1. Open vmui

The Mandate `victoriametrics` publishes the in-cluster query address in `status.query.url` ([`nereus mandate get`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#mandate-get)). From your machine, forward a port to it, then open `http://localhost:8428/vmui`. The `--context` names the cluster `nereus init` made.

```bash
kubectl port-forward service/vmsingle-nereus 8428:8428 \
  --context k3d-nereus \
  --namespace nereus-system
```

### 2. Count each Nereid's passes

The queries are [MetricsQL](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/metricsql/), a superset of PromQL. Each Nereid built on nereid-sdk serves its metrics with the label `nereid`, taken from its Pod, so no Pod can pose as a Nereid. One series per Nereid: its reconcile passes since it started.

```text
sum by (nereid) (nereus_nereid_reconcile_total)
```

### 3. See which failed, and why

A Nereid that never failed has no error series, so `or` adds a zero for it from the passes, and every Nereid shows up.

```text
sum by (nereid) (nereus_nereid_reconcile_errors_total) or sum by (nereid) (nereus_nereid_reconcile_total) * 0
```

The errors carry a `reason` label, the cause of a failed pass: group by `(nereid, reason)` to see them.

### 4. See how long a pass takes

The duration is a histogram. The 95th percentile over the last five minutes, per Nereid:

```text
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (nereid, le) (rate(nereus_nereid_reconcile_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
```

## Check it worked

The same port answers the Prometheus query API, for scripts: the first query returns one series per Nereid. A target that fails shows as down, and nothing else stops.

```bash
curl --get \
  --data-urlencode 'query=sum by (nereid) (nereus_nereid_reconcile_total)' \
  http://localhost:8428/api/v1/query
```

## Next

- [Keep a secret](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/secrets/), and [release a chart](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/release/) that reads it.

## Learn more

- [Inside the metrics Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/metrics-reef/): what the Nereid installs, what it scrapes and who reaches it.
- [Runtime and profiles](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/runtime-and-profiles/): why another Nereid of the metrics Reef would publish the same `status.query.url`.

# Connect an organisation

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/scm-connection.md

Connect an organisation of a source host to Nereus through the GitHub App an scm Mandate names: you write the organisation, and the `github` Nereid writes whether the App reaches it. A Connection holds no key and no token.

## Before you start

- The App's Mandate `github`, `Ready`, from [Prove a GitHub App installed](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/access/github-app/). For GitHub to deliver events, give that Mandate the App's webhook secret in `--param webhookSecret=<secret>`.

## Steps

### 1. Apply the scm Reef and the github Nereid

The scm Reef is opt-in, outside the `internal-developer-platform` profile. One `github` Nereid serves both the authentication and the scm Reef.

```bash
nereus reef apply scm
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/reefs/scm created (scm.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1: connections)
```

[`nereus nereid apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/scm.html#apply-github) names both Reefs.

```bash
nereus nereid apply github \
  --reef authentication \
  --reef scm
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/nereids/github created, Ready, pinned to sha256:1e74cbc6a968: see 'nereus authentication --help'
  namespaces/nereus-system-github applied (the github Nereid's Role there, where vault default delivers the App keys)

Next steps:

  nereus mandate create github --reef authentication --nereid github --param appId=<id> --param privateKey=<secret> --param allow=<namespace>:<repository>:<permission>=<level> --default
  nereus mandate create github-scm --reef scm --nereid github --param identity=github --default
```

### 2. Bind the scm Reef to the App

[`nereus mandate create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#mandate-create) binds the scm Reef to the Nereid. Its name follows `<nereid>-<reef>`, and its param `identity` names the App's Mandate; a second App is a second scm Mandate.

```bash
nereus mandate create github-scm \
  --reef scm \
  --nereid github \
  --param identity=github \
  --default
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/mandates/github-scm created (reef: scm, nereid: github, default)
  clusterrole/controller-github configured (nereid github writes the status of mandate github-scm)

Next steps:

  nereus mandate list
```

### 3. Connect the organisations

[`nereus scm connection create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/scm.html#connection-create) names one organisation. The first Connection is the Reef's default; `--mandate` picks another scm Mandate.

```bash
nereus scm connection create example \
  --org example
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ scm/connections/example created (mandate github-scm)

Next steps:

  nereus scm connection get example
```

Connect `labs`, `meta` and `some` the same way, with `--org example-labs`, `example-meta` and `example-some`. A second `--default` is refused: one in the Reef.

```bash
nereus scm connection create other \
  --org example-other \
  --default
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✗ scm/connections/example is the reef's default already: one in the reef. Nothing was changed.
```

## Check it worked

[`nereus scm connection list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/scm.html#connection-list) shows what the App reaches on each organisation. There is no `verify`: the status is the check, from the first that fails: `NotInstalled`, `NotAllRepositories`, `MissingPermissions` (less than `metadata` and `contents` read), else `Ready`.

```bash
nereus scm connection list
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
CONNECTION  ORG           MANDATE     STATUS              DEFAULT
example     example       github-scm  Ready               yes
labs        example-labs  github-scm  NotInstalled        no
meta        example-meta  github-scm  MissingPermissions  no
some        example-some  github-scm  NotAllRepositories  no
```

`nereus scm connection get` says what to do about a status.

```bash
nereus scm connection get labs
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
Name:          labs
Org:           example-labs
Mandate:       github-scm
Nereid:        github
Default:       no
Status:        NotInstalled
Installation:  -
Repositories:  -
Permissions:   -
Message:       the App of mandate github is not installed on the organisation example-labs: install it at https://github.com/apps/example-nereus/installations/new
```

The App's webhook points at `POST /scm/webhook` on the github Nereid's Service, reached only inside the cluster for now: a delivery is accepted only when `X-Hub-Signature-256` checks with the App's `webhookSecret`.

## Clean up

[`nereus scm connection delete`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/scm.html#connection-delete) removes the Connection; the App stays installed on the organisation, and its Mandate in the authentication Reef.

```bash
nereus scm connection delete labs
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ scm/connections/labs deleted

Next steps:

  nereus scm connection list
```

## Next

- [Mirror a repository](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/scm-mirror/) of a connected organisation into the cluster.

## Learn more

- [The scm Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/scm/): Connections and Mirrors, every command.
- [Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/): why a Mandate holds the App, never the Connection.

# Mirror a repository

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/scm-mirror.md

Copy a public Git repository into the cluster, where the `forgejo` Nereid keeps it in a Forgejo it runs, pulled again on an interval. A public source needs no [Connection](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/scm-connection/) and no App.

## Before you start

- The release Reef with the flux Nereid, and the secrets Reef with the openbao Nereid and the vault `default`: Forgejo comes from its upstream chart through the release Reef, and its admin is sealed into the vault.
- The profile `internal-developer-platform` brings the scm Reef and the forgejo Nereid already: then go to step 2.

## Steps

### 1. Apply the scm Reef and the forgejo Nereid

```bash
nereus reef apply scm
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/reefs/scm created (scm.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1: connections)
```

[`nereus nereid apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/scm.html#mirror-apply) installs the Nereid. It makes its own Mandate `forgejo`, asks the release Reef for Forgejo (SQLite on a volume, no Ingress) and makes Forgejo's admin.

```bash
nereus nereid apply forgejo \
  --reef scm
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/nereids/forgejo created, Ready: see 'nereus scm --help'
  core/mandates/forgejo created (reef: scm, nereid: forgejo)

Next steps:

  nereus scm mirror create <name> --from https://github.com/<owner>/<repository>
```

Forgejo copies from `github.com` only. The Nereid's setting `MIRROR_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` adds hosts, comma-separated (`--set MIRROR_ALLOWED_DOMAINS=git.example.com`).

### 2. Mirror a repository

[`nereus scm mirror create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/scm.html#mirror-create) copies the repository at `--from`, pulled again every `--interval`. It goes through `--mandate`, else the Reef's default Mandate; a Mandate whose Nereid serves no mirrors, such as `github-scm`, is refused.

```bash
nereus scm mirror create nereus \
  --from https://github.com/getnereus/nereus \
  --interval 10m
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ scm/mirrors/nereus created (mandate forgejo)

Next steps:

  nereus scm mirror get nereus
```

A source is `https://`. A plain `http://` host in the cluster needs both `--allow-http` here and the setting `MIRROR_ALLOW_HTTP=true` on the Nereid.

## Check it worked

[`nereus scm mirror list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/scm.html#mirror-list) shows the commit each copy holds: `Syncing` until the first pull, then `Ready`.

```bash
nereus scm mirror list
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
MIRROR   FROM                                       MANDATE  LAST SYNC             COMMIT   STATUS
nereus   https://github.com/getnereus/nereus        forgejo  2026-11-10T12:00:00Z  68d7a0d  Ready
outside  https://example.com/example/outside        forgejo  -                     -        SourceUnreachable
```

`nereus scm mirror get` adds the address the cluster clones from, and the default branch.

```bash
nereus scm mirror get nereus
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
Name:         nereus
From:         https://github.com/getnereus/nereus
Interval:     10m
Mandate:      forgejo
Nereid:       forgejo
Status:       Ready
Repository:   getnereus/nereus
Clone:        http://forgejo-http.nereus-system-forgejo.svc:3000/getnereus/nereus.git
Branch:       main
Commit:       68d7a0d6f1c2b3a4d5e6f708192a3b4c5d6e7f80
Last sync:    2026-11-10T12:00:00Z
Message:      getnereus/nereus holds 68d7a0d6f1c2 of main, pulled every 10m.
```

Any other status names what to fix:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `SourceUnreachable` | a host outside `MIRROR_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`, a repository that is not there, or a plain `http://` source without `MIRROR_ALLOW_HTTP` |
| `Taken` | another Mirror, the oldest, holds the same `<owner>/<repository>`, or Forgejo holds one there copied from another source |
| `NoMandate` | no scm Mandate names the forgejo Nereid |
| `WaitingForForgejo` | Forgejo is not up yet; the message gives the reason the Mandate `forgejo` carries |

## Clean up

`nereus scm mirror delete` removes the copy in Forgejo too, never the source.

```bash
nereus scm mirror delete nereus
```

## Next

- [Connect an organisation](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/scm-connection/) to reach its private repositories through a GitHub App.

## Learn more

- [The scm Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/scm/): Connections and Mirrors, every command.

# Send messages

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/messaging.md

Give a project a topic and a queue on NATS, each with a Secret that says where to reach it, made by the `nats` Nereid. The Mandate picks the Nereid, so the code asks for an engine, never for a server.

A topic carries each message to everyone who listens, on the subject `topics.<name>`. A queue keeps each message until one worker takes it, in the JetStream stream `queue-<name>` on `queues.<name>`. To put a coding agent in the team's room, see [Join the team's room](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/team-room/).

## Before you start

- A cluster from [Prepare the cluster](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init/), with the [tenancy tree](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/tenancy-and-access/) its profile seeds: the owner of each topic and queue, here the project `triton`, must exist in it.

## Steps

### 1. Apply the messaging Reef

[`nereus reef apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/messaging.html#apply-reef) brings the two kinds.

```bash
nereus reef apply messaging
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/reefs/messaging 0.1.0 created (messaging.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1: queues, topics)

Next steps:

  nereus messaging --help
  nereus nereid apply <nereid> --reef messaging
```

### 2. Apply the nats Nereid and its Mandate

[`nereus nereid apply nats`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/messaging.html#apply-nats) runs NATS next to the Nereid in its Pod, with JetStream on the claim `nats-data`.

```bash
nereus nereid apply nats \
  --reef messaging
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/nereids/nats created, Ready, pinned to sha256:<digest>: see 'nereus messaging --help'

Next steps:

  nereus mandate create messaging-nats --reef messaging --nereid nats --match engine=nats --param jetstream=true
```

The Mandate takes every request of engine `nats`; `jetstream=true` is what queues need. A second Mandate with the same match is refused.

```bash
nereus mandate create messaging-nats \
  --reef messaging \
  --nereid nats \
  --match engine=nats \
  --param jetstream=true
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/mandates/messaging-nats created (reef: messaging, nereid: nats, match: engine=nats)
```

### 3. Create a topic

[`nereus messaging topic create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/messaging.html#topic-create) names the owner and the engine. An owner missing from the tree is refused before anything is written.

```bash
nereus messaging topic create orders \
  --owner project/triton \
  --engine nats
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ messaging/topics/orders created (mandate: messaging-nats, nereid: nats)

Next steps:

  nereus messaging topic get orders
```

### 4. Create a queue

[`nereus messaging queue create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/messaging.html#queue-create) takes the same flags.

```bash
nereus messaging queue create builds \
  --owner project/triton \
  --engine nats
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ messaging/queues/builds created (mandate: messaging-nats, nereid: nats)

Next steps:

  nereus messaging queue get builds
```

### 5. Create one from a file

A dry run writes the YAML that [`nereus messaging queue apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/messaging.html#queue-apply) takes. `--deletion-policy delete` drops the stream and its messages with the queue; `retain`, the default, keeps them.

```bash
nereus messaging queue create scratch \
  --owner project/triton \
  --engine nats \
  --deletion-policy delete \
  --dry-run \
  --output yaml > scratch.yaml
```

```bash
nereus messaging queue apply \
  --from-file scratch.yaml
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ messaging/queues/scratch created

Next steps:

  nereus messaging queue list
```

A topic works the same way, with `nereus messaging topic apply`.

## Check it worked

`nereus messaging topic list` and `nereus messaging queue list` show each one `Ready`, with the Mandate and the Nereid that took it. [`nereus messaging queue get`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/messaging.html#queue-get) names the Secret that says where to reach it: `builds-queue` in `nereus-system`, with the keys `host`, `port`, `uri`, `subject` and `stream`.

## Clean up

[`nereus messaging queue delete`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/messaging.html#queue-get) follows the queue's deletion policy.

```bash
nereus messaging queue delete builds
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ messaging/queues/builds deleted (deletionPolicy: retain, its messages are kept)

Next steps:

  nereus messaging queue list
```

```bash
nereus messaging queue delete scratch
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ messaging/queues/scratch deleted (deletionPolicy: delete)

Next steps:

  nereus messaging queue list
```

```bash
nereus messaging topic delete orders
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ messaging/topics/orders deleted (deletionPolicy: retain, its messages are kept)

Next steps:

  nereus messaging topic list
```

## Next

- [Join the team's room](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/team-room/): a coding agent's session on the same NATS.

## Learn more

- [The messaging Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/messaging/): topics, queues and sessions, every command.
- [Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/): why the Mandate, not the code, picks NATS.

# Join the team's room

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/team-room.md

Put your coding agent in the team's room on Triton, where the agents of the team's people say what they claim, ask and release. There is no room to create and no invitation to send: an admin gives you access, then you join alone.

## Before you start

- The CLI from [Install the CLI](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/install/) and Claude Code, logged in with `claude auth login`. No cluster, kubeconfig or NATS.
- Your e-mail with the admin of the installation, here `alice@example.com`.

## Steps

### 1. The admin lets you in

The admin adds your e-mail to the keycloak Mandate's `googleUsers`: the list is the invitation. The keycloak Nereid makes your user, and on your first Google login you choose a username.

```bash
nereus mandate apply keycloak \
  --reef authentication \
  --nereid keycloak \
  --param googleTeam=alice@example.com,bob@example.com
```

`googleTeam` lists the e-mails of the team: the keycloak Nereid makes each one a user (no need to repeat it in `googleUsers`) and puts it in the group `nereus-team`; an e-mail dropped from the list leaves the group. A login outside the group reaches Triton but no tool. Nobody touches Keycloak's console.

### 2. Log in to the installation

[`nereus login`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/authentication.html#login) opens a browser page. On a machine with no browser (a container, SSH), add `--use-device-code`: the terminal shows a page and a code to open on another device.

```bash
nereus login https://nereus.example.com
```

### 3. Work in a clone of the repository

Without a room named, the room is the name of the folder's git `origin`: a clone of `nereus.git` is in the room `nereus`. A room is a Room of the rooms Reef; Triton serves only the Rooms that exist, and a refusal lists them. A team member makes another with `nereus rooms create` ([Create a room for your team](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/rooms/)).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/getnereus/nereus.git
```

### 4. Start your agent in the room

[`nereus rooms join`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#join) opens Claude Code in this terminal under a Nereid's name no agent holds on Triton, with the room's peer tools under your own login and a hook that reads the room's new messages at each prompt. `--tmux` names the tmux window after it; `--name` picks the agent's name.

```bash
nereus rooms join \
  --tmux
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
no name given: the agent is speo (a Nereid's name, free on Triton)
  peer: rooms/peers/alice.speo in nereus
  wake: a message to speo wakes this session (channel nereus-local)
starting speo with claude-code: in the room nereus on Triton
```

A message addressed to your agent (`nereus rooms post --to alice/speo`, or a peer's `post_room` with `to`) wakes it even when idle, as a turn of its own: a direct `claim`, `ask`, `note` or `release`.

Every other message, those to the whole room and the answers `ok`, `wait` and `decided`, waits for the agent's next tool result or prompt, and nothing forces a reply. `--no-wake` leaves the wake off.

To join from a Claude Code session already open, its agent runs `nereus rooms join` from its Bash tool, with no restart, but with no wake until restarted by `nereus rooms join`; that needs [`nereus mcp local add`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#mcp-local) once, which puts the room's tools and hooks in Claude Code's user scope.

## Check it worked

[`nereus rooms follow`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#follow) shows the room yourself, without an agent: the last 10 minutes, then each new message until Ctrl-C, or with `--once` what the room holds.

```bash
nereus rooms follow \
  --room nereus \
  --since 15m \
  --once
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
21:02:11  alice/speo  claim    #1406 in ../nereus-1406-size, paths controllers/vcluster/
21:02:40  bob/doto    note     k3d-nereus is mine until 21:30
21:30:02  bob/doto    release  k3d-nereus
```

[`nereus rooms peer list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#peer-list) shows your agent as a Peer under your username, and [`nereus rooms post`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#post) says something to the room with no agent.

## Next

- Follow the protocol the agents use in the room, `[claim]`, `[ask]`, `[ok]`, `[wait]`, `[note]` and `[release]`, the same as between the sessions of one machine.

## Learn more

- [The rooms Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/rooms/): rooms, peers, room sessions and the conversation, every command.
- [Triton](https://github.com/getnereus/nereus/tree/main/controllers/triton): the room, the peer messages and their limits.

# Create a room for your team

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/rooms.md

Give your team a room of its own on Triton, beside the repository's: a Room of the rooms Reef, owned by your team's project, which Triton backs with a Topic of the messaging Reef. A member of the team creates it with no admin, and every member's agent can join it.

## Before you start

- You are in the team's room already: [Join the team's room](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/team-room/) (the CLI, `nereus login`, and your login in the group `nereus-team`).
- The installation has the rooms Reef and Triton (`nereus reef list` shows `rooms`).

## Steps

### 1. Create the room

[`nereus rooms create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#room-create) makes the Room; without `--owner`, the current owner (`nereus config set owner`), else your team's owner. Triton applies its Topic, `room-<room>`, closed to every other client.

```bash
nereus rooms create ops \
  --owner project/payments \
  --description "Operations peers"
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ rooms/rooms/ops created (owner: project/payments)

Next steps:

  nereus rooms get ops
```

Past the default Mandate's `maxRooms`, 20 by default, the command refuses and names what an admin runs to raise it.

### 2. Put your agent in it

[`nereus rooms join`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#join) opens Claude Code with an agent in the room. From a session already open, its agent runs the same command from its Bash tool and joins one more room with no restart; [`nereus rooms leave`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#leave) takes it out of one room and keeps it in the others.

```bash
nereus rooms join ops
```

### 3. Tell the room without an agent

[`nereus rooms post`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#post) posts as you, with no agent's session.

```bash
nereus rooms post "k3d-nereus is mine until 21:30" \
  --room ops
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ rooms/rooms/ops note posted (id m-20261122-0128)
```

## Check it worked

[`nereus rooms get`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#room-list) shows the Room, its Ready Peers and whether its Topic is ready; [`nereus rooms follow --room ops`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#follow) shows its messages.

```bash
nereus rooms get ops
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
NAME  OWNER             DESCRIPTION       PEERS  MESSAGES  READY
ops   project/payments  Operations peers  2      -         True

PEERS: ana.doto (Ready), bia.speo (Ready)
```

[`nereus rooms session list --room ops`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#session-list) shows each room session, from the first peer in to the last one out, which Triton writes as a `RoomSession`. The messages stay on the Topic while its retention keeps them; there is no file of them yet.

## Clean up

[`nereus rooms delete ops --yes`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/rooms.html#room-delete) removes the Room and its Topic; with `deletionPolicy: retain`, the default, the engine keeps the messages. Only admins delete a room for now.

## Next

- [Join the team's room](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/team-room/): the walkthrough for a new person of the team.

## Learn more

- [The rooms Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/rooms/): rooms, peers, room sessions and the conversation, every command.
- [Triton](https://github.com/getnereus/nereus/tree/main/controllers/triton): the rooms Reef's Nereid.

# Use the MCP server

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/mcp.md

Reach the tools of the installed Reefs from Claude Code or claude.ai: the [Nereus API](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/nereus-api/) serves `/mcp` itself, each tool run as you, through the installation's entrance as `/v1` is.

## Before you start

- An installation reachable at `https://nereus.example.com`, and `nereus login` done, from [Turn on authentication](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/access/authentication/).
- To choose the tools the installation offers, a login in `nereus-admins`.

## Steps

### 1. See the tools you may call

[`nereus mcp tool list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#mcp-tool-list) shows each tool the installed Reefs declare whose route you may call, the core's `status` first. A tool whose route is a `POST` shows `off (write)`: it starts off until an admin enables it.

```bash
nereus mcp tool list
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
REEF           TOOL                STATE
core           status              on
presentations  presentations_list  on
```

### 2. Choose the tools the installation offers

An admin turns tools off or on with [`nereus mcp tool disable` and `enable`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#mcp-tool-switch), by name or every tool of a Reef (`<reef>_*`). An exact name beats a pattern.

```bash
nereus mcp tool disable presentations_list
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ tool presentations_list disabled for the instance
```

```bash
nereus mcp tool enable 'presentations_*'
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ tools presentations_* enabled for the instance
! presentations_list stays off: disabled by its own name, which beats a pattern
```

The switch lives in the `Installation`'s `spec.mcp.tools`; `/mcp` lists and calls only the tools `on`, and the list shows the others as `off (instance)`. It is never changed through `/mcp` itself.

### 3. Add it to Claude Code

[`nereus mcp client add`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#mcp-client-add) runs Claude Code's own `claude mcp add`, so it never writes the agent's settings or copies your token into them. `--dry-run` shows that command; `--scope user`, the default, adds the server to every project.

```bash
nereus mcp client add claude-code \
  --dry-run
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
would run: claude mcp add --transport http --scope user --client-id claude-code --callback-port 33418 nereus https://nereus.example.com/mcp
```

```bash
nereus mcp client add claude-code
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ claude-code: MCP server nereus added (https://nereus.example.com/mcp, scope user, OAuth client claude-code)

Next steps:

  claude    # then /mcp, and log in to nereus
```

In Claude Code, `/mcp` opens the realm's login page in the browser.

A chat that needs only some Reefs takes a server of its own with `--reef`, named `nereus-<reefs>`: its URL carries `?reefs=`, so it offers only those Reefs' tools and the core's, whose generic reads reach only those Reefs (#2296). A Reef the instance lacks is refused at the connection, naming the installed ones.

```bash
nereus mcp client add claude-code \
  --reef edge,catalog
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ claude-code: MCP server nereus-edge-catalog added (https://nereus.example.com/mcp?reefs=edge,catalog, scope user, OAuth client claude-code)

Next steps:

  claude    # then /mcp, and log in to nereus-edge-catalog
```

### 4. Add it to claude.ai

In claude.ai, add a custom connector with the URL `https://nereus.example.com/mcp` (or `https://nereus.example.com/mcp?reefs=edge,catalog` for a subset, which keeps a chat on the phone light) and the OAuth Client ID `claude`. The client finds the issuer from the protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) and logs in with a token only `/mcp` accepts.

```bash
curl --silent https://nereus.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp
```

``` { .json .output title="output" }
{"resource":"https://nereus.example.com/mcp","authorization_servers":["https://auth.example.com/realms/nereus"],"scopes_supported":["openid","offline_access"],"bearer_methods_supported":["header"]}
```

## Check it worked

After the login, the Claude Code session lists the same tools as `nereus mcp tool list`. `/mcp` is stateless: a Reef installed or uninstalled shows on the client's next connection. `nereus mcp client list` shows the coding agents that have it, one row per server.

```bash
nereus mcp client list
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
CLIENT       SERVER               REEFS          URL                                                SCOPE
claude-code  nereus               all            https://nereus.example.com/mcp                     user
claude-code  nereus-edge-catalog  edge, catalog  https://nereus.example.com/mcp?reefs=edge,catalog  user
```

## Clean up

```bash
nereus mcp client remove claude-code
nereus mcp client remove claude-code --reef edge,catalog
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ claude-code: MCP server nereus removed
✓ claude-code: MCP server nereus-edge-catalog removed
```

## Next

- [Join the team's room](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/team-room/): your coding agent among the team's agents.

## Learn more

- [ADR 0029](https://docs.getnereus.dev/adr/0029-mcp-tools/): each Reef declares its tools in its Nereid's contract, and the Nereus API serves them.

# Follow your agent's quota

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/reefs/usage.md

Report the share of a coding agent's quota window you read, and see where it is heading: the forecast at the reset, its pace, today's goal and the week day by day.

## Before you start

- A cluster from [Prepare the cluster](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init/) with `--profile internal-developer-platform`: it brings the usage Reef with its Nereid `reference-usage`.
- `nereus login` done: the readings go through the Nereus API.
- The share used and the reset of the window, as your agent's status line shows them.

## Steps

### 1. Report a reading

[`nereus usage report`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/usage.html#usage-report) sends the share, read now. Within one window the higher share is kept: an idle session that reports an older, lower share changes nothing.

```bash
nereus usage report weekly \
  --used 75 \
  --resets-at 2026-11-16T01:00:00-03:00
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ usage/windows/weekly reported (75% used, resets Mon 16/11 01:00)

Next steps:

  nereus usage get weekly
```

### 2. Read where it is heading

[`nereus usage get`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/reefs/usage.html#usage-get) shows the forecast at the reset and its pace (`push` below 70%, `steady` up to 99%, `slow` above), today's goal, and the week: the days gone (`~` when estimated), today and the plan for the days left.

Each day reads against its adjusted goal: today's goal as it was fixed at the day's start, what was used then plus what is left to 100% spread over the worked time left.

TOTAL is the share at the day's end (projected for the days ahead, `~`), ADJUSTED that goal (today: the path to it now), GAP the total less the goal, ALLOWED the goal less the day's start, and SPENT what the day used.

```bash
nereus usage get weekly
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
WINDOW  USED  RESETS           FORECAST  PACE    TODAY  READ
weekly  75%   Mon 16/11 01:00  91%       steady  ≤75%   Sat 19:06

DAY        TOTAL  ADJUSTED  GAP  ALLOWED  SPENT
Mon 09/11  10%    11%       -1   +9%      +10%
Tue 10/11  ~21%   21%       ±0   +11%     ~+11%
Wed 11/11  31%    36%       -5   +15%     +10%
Thu 12/11  41%    42%       -1   +11%     +10%
Fri 13/11  60%    56%       +4   +15%     +19%
Sat 14/11  75%    70%       +5   +15%     +15%   today, goal 75%
Sun 15/11  ~91%   100%      -9   +25%     ~+13%  plan
```

### 3. Cut the days where you live

The days and the times are cut in the time zone of the Reef's Mandate. [`nereus init`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#init-profile) sets it on install: the `spec.timeZone` of the `Installation` in `~/.config/nereus/init.yaml` when you set one, else the machine's (`TZ`, then `/etc/localtime`, then `timedatectl`), which it writes back to the file.

It prints the zone and where it came from, and warns when it found none: the days are then cut in UTC.

```text
✓ time zone America/Sao_Paulo (discovered from /etc/localtime; set spec.timeZone of the Installation in ~/.config/nereus/init.yaml to choose it)
```

A Mandate that exists keeps its params, so on an older install set the zone on it by hand. [`nereus mandate apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#mandate-apply) replaces every param, so name them all.

```bash
nereus mandate apply reference-usage \
  --reef usage \
  --nereid reference-usage \
  --default \
  --param timeZone=America/Sao_Paulo
```

### 4. Report a reset

When the quota was reset and the share really went down, say so with `--replace`: the lower share wins, and the days gone stay. For an hour, a reading above it but not above the old peak is taken for a stale session's and ignored.

```bash
nereus usage report weekly \
  --used 91 \
  --resets-at 2026-11-16T01:00:00-03:00 \
  --replace
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ usage/windows/weekly replaced 98% (91% used, resets Mon 16/11 01:00), forecast 110.7% slow

Next steps:

  nereus usage get weekly
```

### 5. Report from the status line

`report` keeps a local cache, one JSON file per window under `~/.local/state/nereus/usage/`, and sends at most every 3 minutes (`nereus config set usage_send_interval <interval>` changes it, at least `1m`), so a status line can run it on every reading and read the figures back with `jq`. Offline, the cache keeps the reading and `get` answers from it, marked `local`.

```bash
jq '.figures.forecast' ~/.local/state/nereus/usage/weekly.json
```

## Check it worked

`nereus usage get weekly` shows the share you reported, its forecast, and today never below zero after a reset.

```bash
nereus usage get weekly
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
WINDOW  USED  RESETS           FORECAST  PACE  TODAY  READ
weekly  91%   Mon 16/11 01:00  111%      slow  ≤92%   Sat 19:06

DAY        TOTAL  ADJUSTED  GAP  ALLOWED  SPENT
Mon 09/11  ~18%   13%       +5   +13%     ~+18%
Tue 10/11  ~36%   31%       +5   +13%     ~+18%
Wed 11/11  ~55%   48%       +7   +12%     ~+19%
Thu 12/11  ~73%   66%       +7   +11%     ~+18%
Fri 13/11  91%    81%       +10  +8%      +18%
Sat 14/11  91%    91%       ±0   +1%      +0%    today, goal 92%
Sun 15/11  ~111%  100%      +11  +8%      ~+17%  plan
```

## Next

- [The usage Reef's commands](https://docs.getnereus.dev/reference/reefs/usage/), with `apply`, `list` and `delete`.

# Run the CLI from a checkout

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/cli-checkout.md

Put `nereus` on the `PATH` from a checkout of the repository, editable: a change in `cli/` takes effect at the next run.

## Before you start

- A checkout of `github.com/getnereus/nereus` and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

## Steps

### 1. Install it editable

```bash
make cli
```

It also installs `nrs`, the same program under a short name for typing ([#606](https://github.com/getnereus/nereus/issues/606)). It replaces any other `nereus` installed with `uv tool`.

### 2. Turn on Tab completion

From bash or zsh, for `nereus` and `nrs`, then open a new terminal:

```bash
nereus --install-completion
```

`nrs <Tab>` lists the commands, `nrs nereid apply --<Tab>` the options, and `nrs reef get <Tab>` the Reefs the CLI last saw on the cluster, with no call to it ([#795](https://github.com/getnereus/nereus/issues/795)).

## Check it worked

[`nereus --help`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#groups) lists the command groups. `git pull` updates the CLI; `nereus upgrade` refuses an editable install.

## Clean up

`make cli-uninstall` removes `nereus` and `nrs`.

## Next

[Prepare the cluster](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init/): a checkout's `init` installs the Nereids from the local registry, after `make nereids`.

## Learn more

- [Start a new Nereid](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/new-nereid/) from the template.
- [Keep the CLI up to date](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/operate/cli-update/), for a CLI installed from a release.

# Start a new Nereid

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/new-nereid.md

Render a new [Nereid](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/) from the template: a skeleton that already reports `Ready`, serves its metrics and passes its tests, so you only write the Tool's work.

## Before you start

- A checkout of Nereus, with `uv` on the `PATH`: the template runs through [Copier](https://copier.readthedocs.io/), pinned and run by `uvx`, so there is nothing else to install.
- The Reef the Nereid looks after, and the Tool it drives: here the `edge` Reef and Caddy.

## Steps

### 1. Render the skeleton

`scripts/nereid/new` renders `templates/nereid` into `controllers/<tool>/` and refuses a folder that exists.

```bash
scripts/nereid/new --reef edge --tool caddy
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ controllers/caddy/ created from templates/nereid (copier 9.19.1)
  server.py            the reconcile loop on nereid-sdk, Ready, status.kinds, GET /metrics, the commands' HTTP server
  kube.py              the Kubernetes API, standard library
  requirements.txt     nereid-sdk==0.6.0 (#754), pinned
  Dockerfile           edge-caddy-controller, nereid-sdk from the build context (#741)
  README.md            what the Nereid does, and what every Nereid must do
  test_server.py       the loop's tests, a failing pass counted with its reason
  .copier-answers.yml  the answers, for copier update
Next steps:
  add caddy to NEREIDS in the Makefile, its tests and lint to make test and make lint
  make nereids
  nereus nereid apply caddy --reef edge --image localhost:5111/caddy-controller:0.1.0
```

By default it serves the kind `<reef>s`; `--kinds hostnames,certificates` names the Reef's kinds it serves instead.

### 2. Write the Tool's work

The Tool's work goes in `reconcile()` of `server.py`. The generated `README.md` lists what every Nereid must do: serve every verb of every kind of its Reef, with the status its contract declares.

### 3. Wire it into the build

Add `caddy` to `NEREIDS` in the `Makefile`, and its tests and lint to `make test` and `make lint`, as the skeleton's next steps say.

### 4. Take a later change of the template

From the root of a clean checkout, Copier brings a change of the template as a diff that keeps the Nereid's own changes:

```bash
uvx copier==9.19.1 update \
  --defaults \
  --vcs-ref HEAD \
  controllers/caddy
```

## Check it worked

The skeleton's tests run on the library of the checkout, as the other Nereids' do in `make test`:

```bash
uv run --project cli --with lib/nereid pytest -q controllers/caddy
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
..............                                                           [100%]
14 passed in 0.18s
```

`make nereid-check`, part of `make test`, fails when a Nereid does not pin `nereid-sdk` at the version of `lib/nereid/pyproject.toml`, in `requirements.txt` and in its `Dockerfile`, or does not import `nereid.held`, or rewrites a `Ready` condition's `lastTransitionTime` (below).

A Nereid lists its objects through `held.actionable(items)`, so it never acts on a held object (ADR 0031: no status, no finalizer while the Nereus API's hold is on, #2214). The skeleton does already; `scripts/nereid/held-allowlist` names the Nereids not adopted yet, a list that only shrinks.

A Nereid sets each object's `Ready` condition through `operations.ready(item, status, ready, reason, message, now)`, which keeps the stored `lastTransitionTime` while `Ready`'s status stays the same, so a pass that changes another field never moves it (#2242).

`make nereid-check` fails on a Nereid that compares statuses without `lastTransitionTime` (the mark of a status built with `now`) and does not import `nereid.operations`; `scripts/nereid/ready-allowlist` names the ones not adopted yet, a list that only shrinks.

## Next

- [Build a Nereid's image](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/image/), with the labels that name its Reef, and apply it.
- [Require a Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/requires/) when the Nereid needs another Reef's work.
- [Pass the conformance tests](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/conformance/): every verb of every kind of its Reef.

## Learn more

- [Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/): what a Nereid looks after.
- [Spec 0003](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/0003-nereid-conformance/): the contract a Nereid honours.

# Build a Nereid's image

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/image.md

Build a Nereid's image whose labels name its Reef, push it to the local registry and apply it: the CLI reads the labels before anything runs in the cluster.

## Before you start

- A cluster from [Prepare the cluster](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/init/): `nereus init` creates the local registry `localhost:5111`.
- The Reef applied, here `release`: [Apply your first Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/start/first-reef/).
- Docker, to build and push. The example is the reference Nereid of `controllers/reference`, whose commands only simulate output.

## Steps

### 1. Declare the Reef in labels

The `Dockerfile` names the Reef the Nereid looks after, the Reefs it requires, its name and its version:

```dockerfile
LABEL ${API_GROUP}/reef=${REEF} \
      ${API_GROUP}/requires=${REQUIRES} \
      ${API_GROUP}/nereid=${NEREID} \
      ${API_GROUP}/reference=${REFERENCE} \
      org.opencontainers.image.version=${VERSION} \
      org.opencontainers.image.title=${TITLE}
```

`${API_GROUP}` is `core.getnereus.dev`. The reference Nereid's commands are data, in `commands.yaml`, each with its help and an example:

```yaml
- path: [repo, add]
  help: Add a chart repository.
  arguments:
    - name: name
      help: Name of the repository.
    - name: url
      help: URL of the repository.
```

### 2. Build and push

`make reference` builds the image for the `release` Reef and pushes it; a Nereid from the template builds with `make nereids`.

```bash
make reference
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0 pushed: nereus nereid apply --image localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0
```

### 3. Apply it

[`nereus nereid apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#nereid-apply) reads the labels, pins the image to its digest and waits for `Ready`.

```bash
nereus nereid apply reference-release \
  --reef release \
  --image localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/nereids/reference-release created, Ready, pinned to sha256:ffb8e8957c6e: see 'nereus release --help'

Next steps:

  nereus nereid list
```

### 4. Move it to a new image

Applied again with another image, the Nereid is updated in place; `--dry-run` shows what would change and writes nothing.

```bash
nereus nereid apply reference-release \
  --image localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.1 \
  --dry-run
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
Would configure core/nereids/reference-release for reef release: image sha256:ffb8e8957c6e → sha256:3f2a9c1d7e4b.
Nothing changed (--dry-run).
```

Without `--dry-run`, the apply waits for the new pod and says what the image was:

```bash
nereus nereid apply reference-release \
  --image localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.1
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/nereids/reference-release configured, Ready, pinned to sha256:3f2a9c1d7e4b (was sha256:ffb8e8957c6e): see 'nereus release --help'
```

## Check it worked

[`nereus nereid list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#nereid-list) shows the Nereid `Ready` on its Reef:

```bash
nereus nereid list
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
NEREID             REEFS    IMAGE                                                 STATUS  AGE
reference-release  release  localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0     Ready   10s
openbao            secrets  localhost:5111/openbao-controller:0.1.0               Ready   1m
```

The commands it published are under its Reef: `nereus release --help`.

## Clean up

[`nereus nereid delete`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#nereid-delete) removes it; its Reef stays.

```bash
nereus nereid delete reference-release
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ core/nereids/reference-release deleted
```

## Next

- [Require a Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/requires/): a label that makes one Nereid depend on another Reef.
- [Pass the conformance tests](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/conformance/).

## Learn more

- [Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/).
- [Spec 0003](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/0003-nereid-conformance/): the labels read at install, and what `Ready` means.

# Require a reef

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/requires.md

Make a Nereid require another Reef through a label of its image: the CLI refuses to apply it until that Reef has a Nereid, and refuses to delete that Reef's last Nereid while it is needed.

A Nereid requires Reefs, never Nereids ([spec 0003](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/0003-nereid-conformance/)): any Nereid of the Reef will do.

## Before you start

- The `release` Reef with its Nereid `reference-release`, from [Build a Nereid's image](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/image/).
- An image whose label `core.getnereus.dev/requires` lists the Reefs it needs, comma-separated. Build the reference Nereid as a Nereid of a `docs` Reef that requires `release`: `docker build --build-arg API_GROUP=core.getnereus.dev --build-arg REEF=docs --build-arg REQUIRES=release --tag localhost:5111/reference-docs-controller:0.1.0 controllers/reference`, then `docker push` it.

## Steps

### 1. Create the Reef

[`nereus reef create`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#reef-create) adds the `docs` Reef the new Nereid looks after.

```bash
nereus reef create docs
```

### 2. Apply the Nereid that requires a Reef

[`nereus nereid apply`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#nereid-apply) reads `requires` from the image's labels and records it in the Nereid's `spec.requires`.

```bash
nereus nereid apply reference-docs \
  --reef docs \
  --image localhost:5111/reference-docs-controller:0.1.0
```

`release` has a Nereid, so the apply goes ahead. Without one, it is refused before anything runs, with `reference-docs requires reefs with no Nereid: release.` and the command that applies one. When the required Reef's Nereid is there but not `Ready`, the apply warns and goes ahead.

## Check it worked

[`nereus nereid list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#nereid-list) shows both Nereids `Ready`: `reference-docs` on `docs`, `reference-release` on `release`.

```bash
nereus nereid list
```

## Clean up

`reference-release` is the last Nereid of `release`, which `docs` requires, so [`nereus nereid delete`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#nereid-delete) refuses it first:

```bash
nereus nereid delete reference-release
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✗ reference-release is the last Nereid of reef release, which added Nereids require: reference-docs.
  Remove them first, or go ahead with: nereus nereid delete reference-release --force
```

Delete `reference-docs` first, then the `docs` Reef with [`nereus reef delete`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#reef-delete); `reference-release` stays:

```bash
nereus nereid delete reference-docs
```

```bash
nereus reef delete docs
```

## Next

- [Pass the conformance tests](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/conformance/).
- [When the Nereid stops](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/troubleshoot/nereid-stops/): what a required Reef's Nereid does to its commands.

## Learn more

- [Reef, Nereid and Mandate](https://docs.getnereus.dev/concepts/model/).
- [Spec 0003](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/0003-nereid-conformance/): the labels read at install, `requires` among them.

# Pass the conformance tests

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/conformance.md

Prove that a Nereid serves every verb of every kind of its Reef, with the status its contract declares, before anyone else relies on it.

## Before you start

- A throwaway k3d cluster, never the kept cluster `k3d-nereus`: the check creates and deletes objects, and refuses any other context.
- The Nereid applied and `Ready` ([Build a Nereid's image](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/image/)), and named by the Reef's default Mandate.

## Steps

### 1. Ship a sample per kind

Each kind of the Reef has a sample in its contract, `cli/src/nereus/interfaces/<reef>/samples/<kind>.yaml`: the objects the kind needs first, the object as created, then the same object with a change to its spec. The `release` Reef ships `release.yaml`, `repository.yaml`, `source.yaml` and `target.yaml`.

### 2. Write the status the contract declares

Every object the Nereid answers gets a `Ready` condition whose reason the contract declares, `status.observedGeneration`, and the finalizer `<reef>.getnereus.dev/cleanup`, removed only once what it made is gone. A kind the Nereid does nothing with still answers, with the reason `NotApplicable`.

### 3. Run the check

`test/conformance` drives `nereus` and `kubectl` kind by kind: apply with `--dry-run` then for real, the status checked against the kind's schema, the finalizer, a change, `get`, `list`, then delete.

```bash
test/conformance release --nereid reference-release
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✓ reference-release serves every verb of every kind of the release reef and honours its contract: Release Repository Source Target
```

`--timeout` sets the seconds each wait lasts, 120 by default.

## Check it worked

The last line of the run names every kind it proved; any `FAIL:` line before it names the object, the field and the rule it breaks.

`make scene-release` runs the same check against the reference Nereid, then against `flux`.

## Next

- [See what happened](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/troubleshoot/see-what-happened/) when a step of the check fails.
- [Require a Reef](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/build/requires/).

## Learn more

- [Spec 0003](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/0003-nereid-conformance/): what every Nereid answers, and the check kind by kind.
- [ADR 0013](https://docs.getnereus.dev/adr/0013-command-conventions/): the verbs every kind serves.

# A name is taken

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/troubleshoot/name-taken.md

`nereus init --target azure` stops at the names plan, before it creates anything in Azure.

## You see

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✗ names                         0.1s  storage account issuers0b7e4c1a93d24f6e is taken in Azure
  total                         0.2s  slo 20m, 0% green
  Record it for issuer.storage, then prepare the undercloud again with it:
    nereus config installation set --naming-override issuer.storage=issuers0b7e4c1a93d24f6e2
    nereus init --target azure
```

## Why

A storage account name is unique across Azure, and the issuer's is `issuers<id16>`. The likely owner is a deleted installation with the same id.

## Fix

Record the suggested name with [`nereus config installation set`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#installation-set), then prepare the undercloud again:

```bash
nereus config installation set \
  --naming-override issuer.storage=issuers0b7e4c1a93d24f6e2
nereus init --target azure
```

In a terminal without `--yes`, `init` asks instead, and a yes does the same:

``` { .text .output title="output" }
? Use issuers0b7e4c1a93d24f6e2 for issuer.storage? (Y/n) y
✓ installation tailwind  naming.overrides.issuer.storage = issuers0b7e4c1a93d24f6e2
```

## Check

The next `init` recreates the cluster with the new issuer and runs to the end: every line starts with `✓`.

# When the Nereid stops

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/troubleshoot/nereid-stops.md

A command of a Reef stops at once, sends nothing and exits non-zero, because its Nereid has no pod serving.

## You see

```bash
nereus release repo list
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
✗ nereid reference-release is Unavailable: its Controller has no pod serving.
  Its commands work again by themselves once the Controller is back: see 'nereus nereid list'.
```

[`nereus nereid list`](https://docs.getnereus.dev/specs/cli/core.html#nereid-list) shows the Nereid's `STATUS` as `Unavailable`, computed by the CLI from its Deployment.

## Why

The Nereid's Deployment has no ready pod: scaled to zero, or its pod crashing. A deleted pod is replaced by the Deployment, and the new one starts with an empty work directory.

## Fix

Bring the Deployment back, here scaled up from zero: `kubectl scale deployment reference-release --namespace nereus-system --replicas 1`. For a crashing pod, read why first in [See what happened](https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/troubleshoot/see-what-happened/).

## Check

The same command works again by itself, with no retry flag:

```bash
nereus release repo add chaos-scaled https://charts.example.com
```

``` { .text .output title="output" }
"chaos-scaled" has been added to your repositories
```

`test/scene` kills the pod and scales the Deployment to zero and back, then checks these lines.

# See what happened

Source: https://docs.getnereus.dev/guides/troubleshoot/see-what-happened.md

Find why a Reef, a Nereid or an object is not `Ready`, starting from the CLI and going down to the object's events and the Nereid's log.

## Before you start
